chapters.title: The Alphabet

concepts.name: The Greek alphabet: letters, names, and pronunciation
Vowels (short, long, close, open) and diphthongs
Rough and smooth breathings
The three accents: acute, circumflex, grave (introduced, not yet used)
Greek punctuation marks (comma, period, colon, question mark)

chapters.notes: This lesson covers only the alphabet, vowels, diphthongs, breathings, accents, and punctuation marks; there is no vocabulary section, so generate no vocabulary-based exercises. Practice should focus on letter recognition/formation and pronunciation drills (e.g., reading syllables and short words aloud), not on morphology, syntax, or word meaning.

chapters.title: Accent

concepts.name: Greek accent: acute, circumflex, grave; general rules of accent
Rule of verb accent (recessive accent)
Rule of noun accent (persistent accent, as near as general rules allow)

chapters.notes: Lesson 2 introduces no vocabulary; drills should focus purely on syllable division (ultima/penult/antepenult), vowel/diphthong quantity, and applying the six general accent rules plus the verb (recessive) and noun (persistent) accent rules to given unaccented forms — avoid testing meaning or translation here.
verifier_notes: misses §10 preliminary definitions: ultima/penult/antepenult and syllable quantity (long vowel/diphthong = long; final -αι/-οι count short) — the prerequisite block for every accent rule

chapters.title: Present Active Indicative

concepts.name: Present Active Indicative
Verb stem and personal endings

chapters.notes: Practice should use only present active indicative forms of these eight -ω verbs (no compounds, no other tenses/moods); when drilling 2nd person, note that English 'you' is ambiguous between λύεις (sg.) and λύετε (pl.) unless archaic 'thou/ye' forms are used to disambiguate.
verifier_notes: misses §21: present tense covers both 'I loose' and 'I am loosing' (continuous/progressive force) — an explicit teaching point, not a paradigm detail

chapters.title: The Second Declension. Order of Words. Movable ν.

concepts.name: Second declension nouns (masculine -ος, neuter -ον)
Definite article (gender agreement, no indefinite article)
Uses of the cases: nominative subject, accusative object, genitive possession, dative indirect object, vocative direct address
Normal and variable order of words in a Greek sentence
Movable ν on third person plural verb forms
Second-declension noun accent (circumflex in gen./dat. when ultima accented)

chapters.notes: Practice only second-declension nouns (masc./fem. -ος, neut. -ον) paired with the third-person present active indicative verbs already known (γινώσκει, βλέπει, λέγει, γράφει, διδάσκει, λαμβάνει, λύει, ἔχει); vary subject-verb-object word order for emphasis, use movable ν before vowels or sentence-end with -ουσι(ν) forms, and avoid first/third declension nouns, adjectives, or other moods/tenses not yet introduced.
validation_notes: ἱερόν NOT IN CORPUS (candidates: ἱεροπρεπής, ἱεροσυλέω, ἱερουργέω)
verifier_notes: vocab miss: ἱερόν, τό 'a temple' omitted (lesson §24 lists 12 items, map has 11)
misses §42 neuter rule: in all neuters of all declensions voc./acc. = nom. in both numbers, and neuter nom/voc/acc plural ends in short α

chapters.title: The First Declension

concepts.name: First declension (α/η-stem feminine nouns)
First-declension genitive plural accent exception (circumflex on ultima)

chapters.notes: Practice should drill first-declension feminine nouns (ὥρα/δόξα/γραφή/ἀλήθεια patterns) in all cases and numbers, paired only with present active indicative verbs already known (e.g. βλέπει, γινώσκει, λέγει, διδάσκει, γράφει, ἔχουσι); emphasize the genitive plural circumflex exception and the α vs η alternation in gen./dat. singular, and avoid introducing second/third declension or non-present verb forms.
verifier_notes: misses §55: α of the nominative singular becomes η in gen./dat. sg. except after ε, ι, ρ — the rule that generates the δόξα vs. ὥρα split
misses §58: general first-declension accent rule (circumflex on accented ultima in gen./dat. of both numbers, acute elsewhere); map captured only the §51 gen.-pl. exception

chapters.title: The Article; Adjectives of the First and Second Declension: Agreement, Attributive and Predicate Position, Substantive Use

concepts.name: The article ὁ, ἡ, τό (declension and use)
First/second declension adjectives (-ος, -η/-α, -ον)
Agreement of article and adjective with noun in gender, number, case
Attributive vs. predicate position of the adjective
Substantive use of the adjective

chapters.notes: Practice should pair the article with -ος/-η/-ον adjectives (feminine in α after ρ/vowel, e.g. δικαία, μικρά) in both attributive patterns (ὁ ἀγαθὸς λόγος / ὁ λόγος ὁ ἀγαθός) and predicate patterns (ὁ λόγος ἀγαθός / ἀγαθὸς ὁ λόγος) with copula omitted; include substantive adjective use (οἱ ἀγαθοί, τὰ ἀγαθά). Keep verbs limited to present active indicative (e.g. ἐγείρω, βλέπω, λέγω, γράφω) and avoid introducing new declensions or tenses not yet covered.
verifier_notes: misses §64: definition of proclitic and that ὁ, ἡ, οἱ, αἱ are proclitics — taught here, and Lesson 7 later cites it back
misses §60 note + §62: ἔρημος and ὁδός are feminine despite -ος; and adjective feminine takes long α (not η) after ρ or a vowel

chapters.title: Masculine Nouns of the First Declension; Prepositions

concepts.name: First declension masculine nouns (προφήτης/μαθητής type)
Prepositions and the cases they govern
Genitive of separation, dative of place, accusative of motion toward
Proclitics (ἐν, εἰς, ἐκ)

chapters.notes: Drill the masculine first-declension paradigm (προφήτης/μαθητής: -ης, -ου, -ῃ, -ην, -α sg.; -αι, -ῶν, -αις, -ας pl.) alongside prepositional phrases that fix each preposition to a single case (ἐν+dat, εἰς+acc, ἐκ/ἀπό+gen) or contrast dual-case ones (διά+gen 'through' vs +acc 'on account of'; μετά+gen 'with' vs +acc 'after'). Keep sentences to present-tense indicative verbs already known (ἄγω, βάλλω, μένω, πέμπω, φέρω) so the prepositional phrase is the sole new element being tested.
verifier_notes: concept id GK.ENCLIT is used for proclitics; the lesson teaches proclitics (§84), enclitics are Lesson 8 — content right, id mislabeled

misses §85: prepositions with several cases change meaning by case (διά+gen. 'through' vs +acc. 'on account of'; μετά+gen. 'with' vs +acc. 'after') — the lesson's main preposition point beyond the generic case rule

chapters.title: Enclitics; Personal Pronouns; Present Indicative of εἰμί

concepts.name: Enclitics and their accent rules
Personal pronouns (1st, 2nd, 3rd person declension and use)
Present indicative of εἰμί
Postpositive δέ (cannot stand first in its clause)
Genitive of the personal pronoun expressing possession

chapters.notes: Practice sentences should use unemphatic enclitic pronoun forms (μου, μοι, με, σου, σοι, σε) for possession and object, reserving emphatic forms (ἐμοῦ, ἐμοί, ἐμέ, σοῦ, σοί, σέ) for after prepositions or contrast; avoid nominative ἐγώ/σύ except when emphasis/contrast is intended, since verb endings alone mark person. Reinforce δέ as postpositive (never clause-initial) and drill enclitic accent placement (e.g. ἄνθρωπός μου, ὥρα ἐστίν) alongside αὐτός used only as 3rd-person object/oblique pronoun, not as nominative subject.
verifier_notes: GK.CASE.USES 'genitive of personal pronoun expressing possession' is not supported anywhere in the supplied text (excerpt ends mid-§97); flag as unverified rather than confirmed-invented
GK.PRES.ACT.IND for εἰμί likewise appears only in the lesson title, not the supplied body — same truncation caveat
misses (assuming full lesson) the uses of αὐτός: intensive 'himself', ὁ αὐτός 'the same', attributive/predicate position

chapters.title: Demonstrative Pronouns; Further Uses of αὐτός

concepts.name: Demonstrative pronouns οὗτος (this) and ἐκεῖνος (that): declension and predicate-position agreement with a noun
Further uses of αὐτός: intensive ('-self', predicate position), 'same' (attributive position), and intensive use with pronouns/unexpressed subjects
Predicate vs. attributive position governing demonstratives, intensive αὐτός, and ὁ αὐτός ('same')

chapters.notes: Drill οὗτος/ἐκεῖνος only in predicate position with an articular noun (οὗτος ὁ λόγος / ὁ λόγος οὗτος), and contrast intensive αὐτός ('himself', predicate position) against ὁ αὐτός ('same', attributive position); avoid μι-verbs or new tenses beyond present active/indicative already introduced.

chapters.title: Present Middle and Passive Indicative; ὑπό with the Genitive; the Dative of Means; Deponent Verbs; Compound Verbs; the Position of οὐ

concepts.name: Present Middle Indicative
Present Passive Indicative
ὑπό + genitive (agent), dative of means, and verbs taking genitive/dative objects
Deponent verbs
Compound verbs (preposition + verb)
Position of the negative οὐ

chapters.notes: Practice should contrast present middle/passive forms (identical in the present, so treat ambiguous forms as passive) with active forms already known; drill ὑπό + genitive as personal agent versus the plain dative of means, and highlight deponents like ἔρχομαι-compounds (εἰσέρχομαι, ἐξέρχομαι, διέρχομαι, πορεύομαι, ἀποκρίνομαι) that are passive in form but active in meaning. Avoid introducing middle/passive forms outside the present tense, and keep οὐ placed immediately before the verb it negates.

chapters.title: Imperfect Active Indicative; Imperfect Indicative of εἰμί; Accent of ἔστι(ν)

concepts.name: Imperfect active indicative
Augment (syllabic ἐ- and temporal vowel-lengthening)
Augment placement in compound verbs
Imperfect indicative of εἰμί
Accent of ἔστι(ν) after οὐκ and certain words

chapters.notes: Drill only the imperfect active indicative of regular -ω verbs (including compounds with prepositional prefixes) and the imperfect of εἰμί; keep augment placement after the prefix and before the stem, with prefix-vowel elision, and don't let accent recede past the augment. Avoid the aorist or other tenses (not yet introduced) and use μέν...δέ pairs to contrast past vs. present habitual action, per the lesson's exercises.
verifier_notes: Missing vocab lemma βαίνω ('I go', §121 headword — the simple verb Machen lists alongside ἀναβαίνω/καταβαίνω)

chapters.title: Imperfect Middle and Passive Indicative; Singular Verb with Neuter Plural Subject; Uses of καί and οὐδέ

concepts.name: Imperfect middle indicative
Imperfect passive indicative (middle/passive identical in form)
Neuter plural subject with singular verb
Uses of καί (also, even, καί...καί) and οὐδέ (nor, not even, οὐδέ...οὐδέ)
Deponent verbs retain deponency in the imperfect

chapters.notes: Drill imperfect middle/passive forms of λύω (ἐλυόμην, ἐλύου, ἐλύετο, ἐλυόμεθα, ἐλύεσθε, ἐλύοντο) alongside deponent compounds like ἀπέρχομαι/ἐκπορεύομαι/συνέρχομαι/κατέρχομαι/δέχομαι in the imperfect (e.g. ἠρχόμην); include some neuter plural subjects taking a singular verb (τὰ δαιμόνια ἐξέρχεται) but also show plural agreement as a valid alternative. Practice καί...καί and οὐδέ...οὐδέ correlative pairs plus the adverbial 'also/even' and 'not even' senses; avoid introducing aorist, future, or perfect forms in this lesson's practice.

chapters.title: Future Active and Middle Indicative

concepts.name: Future Active Indicative
Future Middle Indicative
Future of Mute (Labial/Palatal/Lingual) Stems before σ
Deponent Future (deponent in future but not present)
Principal Parts of the Verb

chapters.notes: Drill future active/middle indicative of λύω-type verbs and consonant-stem futures (labial+σ→ψ, palatal+σ→ξ, lingual drops before σ) using §156 rules; present the deponent futures (γενήσομαι, γνώσομαι, λήμψομαι, ἐλεύσομαι, προσεύξομαι, βήσομαι) as memorized principal parts rather than derived forms. Avoid future passive forms entirely, since they are not introduced until a later lesson.
verifier_notes: Missing vocab lemma βαίνω (vocabulary entry βήσομαι, dep. fut. of βαίνω, §150)

chapters.title: First Aorist Active and Middle Indicative; Constructions with πιστεύω

concepts.name: First Aorist Active Indicative
First Aorist Middle Indicative
Constructions with πιστεύω (dative of person; εἰς + accusative for 'believe in/on')

chapters.notes: Introduce only first aorist active and middle indicative (not second aorist, not aorist passive, which come in later lessons); contrast aorist ἔλυσα (simple past) against imperfect ἔλυον (continuous past). Drill πιστεύω with a dative object (I believe the man) versus πιστεύω εἰς + accusative (I believe in/on); avoid mixing in aorist passive or perfect forms.

chapters.title: Second Aorist Active and Middle Indicative

concepts.name: Second aorist active indicative
Second aorist middle indicative

chapters.notes: Drill second aorist active/middle indicative forms only for verbs whose second aorist stem is already given in the vocabulary (ἔβαλον, ἐγενόμην, εἶδον, εἶπον, ἔλαβον, ἤγαγον, ἦλθον, ἔλιπον, ἔπεσον); avoid generating aorist passive forms (not yet taught) and avoid confusing second aorist with imperfect by contrasting stem differences (e.g. ἐλίπομεν vs ἐλείπομεν). Treat ἐγενόμην as deponent (middle form, active sense) and note προσφέρω governs accusative of thing + dative of person.

chapters.title: Aorist Passive Indicative. Future Passive Indicative

concepts.name: Aorist passive indicative
Future passive indicative
Second aorist passive indicative
Deponent verbs with passive (not middle) aorist/future forms

chapters.notes: Drill aorist passive and future passive indicative of λύω-type verbs, using vocabulary items presented as aorist passive forms keyed to their present-tense lemmas (e.g. ἐβλήθην < βάλλω); include a few second aorist passives (θ-less, e.g. ἐγράφην) and deponents with passive-form aorists (ἐγενήθην beside ἐγενόμην) but avoid future/perfect passive stems (4th/5th principal parts) not yet studied. Note ὥφθην is also treated as aor. pass. of ὁράω alongside βλέπω.
verifier_notes: Missing grammar topic: formation of aorist passive stems from consonant-final verb stems (§204: π/β→φ, κ/γ→χ, τ/δ/θ→σ before θη) — the direct parallel of GK.FUT.MUTE.STEM which lesson 13's entry does encode

chapters.title: The Third Declension

concepts.name: Third declension nouns (consonant stems, case endings, dative plural changes)
Monosyllable accent rule: accent on ultima in gen./dat. (circumflex in gen. plur.)

chapters.notes: Practice should stick to third-declension nouns whose genitive singular and gender are given (ἐλπίς/ἐλπίδος, νύξ/νυκτός, ἄρχων/ἄρχοντος, and neuter -μα nouns like ὄνομα/ὀνόματος), always drilling genitive+gender alongside the nominative since the stem and gender cannot be predicted from the nominative alone. Avoid introducing new third-declension nouns without their genitive form, and keep dative plural forms (ἐλπίσι, νυξί, ἄρχουσι) as a focal difficulty.
verifier_notes: Misses the -μα/-ματος neuter noun class (§222), a separately headed topic with its own paradigm (ὄνομα) and the rule that all such nouns are neuter
Minor: misses §§218-219 (gender of 3rd-decl. nouns unpredictable; genitive singular must be learned to find the stem)

chapters.title: Present Participles; Use of Participles

concepts.name: Present active participle (λύων, λύουσα, λῦον)
Present middle/passive participle (λυόμενος, -η, -ον)
Attributive use of the participle
Tense of the participle as relative to the leading verb
Predicate (circumstantial) use of the participle, translated by a temporal clause

chapters.notes: Practice should center on present active and present middle/passive participles of already-known -ω verbs (e.g. λύω, διδάσκω) agreeing in gender/number/case with a noun, in both attributive (ὁ ἀπόστολος ὁ λέγων...) and predicate/circumstantial position (translated with 'while'); use προσέρχομαι with the dative and the irregular participle ὤν, οὖσα, ὄν of εἰμί. Avoid aorist or other non-present participles and avoid indirect discourse constructions, which are not yet introduced.
verifier_notes: Vocabulary miss: ὤν, οὖσα, ὄν (present participle of εἰμί) is in the §225 vocabulary but absent from vocab_lemmas

chapters.title: Aorist Participles Active and Middle; Use of Participles (continued); The Negatives οὐ and μή

concepts.name: Aorist active participle
Aorist middle participle
Second aorist active participle
Second aorist middle participle
Relative time of the aorist participle (action prior to leading verb)
Negatives οὐ and μή

chapters.notes: Drill aorist active and middle participles (λύσας/λυσάμενος) alongside the irregular second aorist participles in this lesson's vocabulary (ἀγαγών, εἰπών, ἐλθών, ἐνεγκών, ἰδών), stressing that the augment is dropped even though it appears in the corresponding aorist indicative. Emphasize translating the aorist participle as action prior to the leading verb ('having done', 'when/after he had...'), both circumstantially and attributively/substantively with the article; avoid perfect or pluperfect participles, which are not yet introduced.

chapters.title: The Aorist Passive Participle; The Genitive Absolute

concepts.name: Aorist passive participle
Genitive absolute construction

chapters.notes: Practice sentences should pair the aorist passive participle (λυθείς type, θε added to the verb stem, irregular non-recessive accent in nom. sg. masc.) with genitive absolute constructions where the participle's subject differs from that of the main verb; use ὑπό + genitive for the agent of the passive action, and avoid genitive absolute when the participial noun/pronoun is coreferential with the main clause subject (use a simple circumstantial participle instead).

chapters.title: The Subjunctive Mood

concepts.name: Present active subjunctive
Present middle/passive subjunctive
Aorist active subjunctive
Aorist middle subjunctive
Aorist passive subjunctive
Second aorist active/middle subjunctive
Hortatory subjunctive (1st pl. exhortation)
Purpose clauses with ἵνα + subjunctive
Future conditions (ἐάν + subj.) vs. other conditions (εἰ + indic.)
Negative μή (and μηδέ, μηκέτι) with the subjunctive

chapters.notes: Prefer aorist subjunctive forms (esp. with ἵνα or ἐάν) over present subjunctive in generated practice, per the book's own guidance that the aorist presents the action more simply; use ἵνα+subjunctive for purpose and ἐάν+subjunctive for future/present-general conditions, contrasting with εἰ+indicative for simple conditions, and negate subjunctives with μή/μηδέ/μηκέτι rather than οὐ; avoid indirect discourse with ὅτι since that is only contrasted here, not taught.
validation_notes: εὐαγγελίζομαι NOT IN CORPUS (candidates: εὐαγγέλιον, εὐαγγελίζω, εὐαγγελιστής)
verifier_notes: Vocabulary miss: εὐαγγελίζομαι is in the §268 vocabulary but absent from vocab_lemmas
Concept miss: §283 'The Tenses in the Subjunctive' — no time distinction, present vs. aorist is aspect only
Concept miss: present subjunctive of εἰμί (§282)

chapters.title: Lesson XXII: The Present and Aorist Infinitives; The Articular Infinitive; Indirect Discourse; Proper Names

concepts.name: Present active infinitive
Present middle/passive infinitive
Aorist active infinitive
Aorist middle infinitive
Aorist passive infinitive
Second aorist active infinitive
Second aorist middle infinitive
Irregular accent of aorist active and passive infinitives
Articular infinitive (as noun, after prepositions, with accusative subject)
Indirect discourse (accusative + infinitive; ὅτι + indicative retaining original tense)
Proper names and the article
Irregular declension of Ἰησοῦς

chapters.notes: Drill present vs. aorist infinitives (active, middle, passive, plus the second-aorist type λιπεῖν/λιπέσθαι) after δεῖ, ἔξεστι, θέλω, μέλλω, ὀφείλω, κελεύω, and the articular infinitive after prepositions (μετὰ τό, πρὸ τοῦ, διὰ τό, ἐν τῷ, εἰς τό for purpose), including infinitives with an accusative subject. For indirect discourse, contrast ὅτι + indicative (retaining the tense of the original direct discourse, unlike English) with the accusative-and-infinitive construction; avoid introducing participial genitive absolutes as substitutes here since the point is the infinitive constructions themselves.
verifier_notes: Vocabulary miss: δεῖ (impersonal, 'it is necessary', takes acc. + infinitive) is the first §292 vocabulary entry but absent from vocab_lemmas
Minor concept miss: negative of the infinitive is μή (§300); present infinitive of εἰμί = εἶναι (§297)

chapters.title: Contract Verbs

concepts.name: Contract verbs in -άω, -έω, -όω and rules of vowel contraction
Accentuation of contracted syllables
Present active indicative of contract verbs
Present middle/passive indicative of contract verbs
Imperfect active indicative of contract verbs
Imperfect middle/passive indicative of contract verbs
Present active infinitive of contract verbs (exceptional contraction -άειν > -ᾶν, -όειν > -οῦν)
Present active participle of contract verbs

chapters.notes: Practice should drill contraction of -άω/-έω/-όω verbs across present and imperfect, all moods and the participle, using only vocabulary items already introduced (e.g. ἀγαπάω, ποιέω, τηρέω, λαλέω); avoid μι-verbs and uncontracted forms, since the uncontracted lexical form is cited only for principal-part purposes and never occurs in running text. Favor short indicative and participial sentences (as in the exercises) that require the learner to apply the accent-of-contraction rules (§III) rather than memorize surface forms.
verifier_notes: Concept miss: §321 principal parts of -άω/-έω/-όω verbs — stem vowel lengthened (α as well as ε → η) before tense suffixes, contraction only in the present system; a headed section of the lesson
Minor: §317 covers the present in all moods studied so far (incl. subjunctive), not just indicative/infinitive/participle as listed

chapters.title: Future and First Aorist Active and Middle of Liquid Verbs; Future of εἰμί; Reflexive and Reciprocal Pronouns

concepts.name: Liquid verbs (stems ending in λ, μ, ν, ρ)
Future active indicative of liquid verbs (-εσ- contracted, conjugated like -έω present)
Future middle indicative of liquid verbs; future of εἰμί
First aorist active of liquid verbs (-α ending, stem lengthened, no σ)
First aorist middle of liquid verbs
Reflexive pronouns ἐμαυτοῦ, σεαυτοῦ, ἑαυτοῦ
Reciprocal pronoun ἀλλήλων
English preparatory 'there' not translated in Greek

chapters.notes: Practice should drill the liquid-verb future/aorist pattern (κρίνω, βάλλω, μένω, ἀποστέλλω, ἐγείρω, ἀποκτείνω, αἴρω, σπείρω) contrasted with regular -σ- futures/aorists already known; keep the future of εἰμί (ἔσομαι) as a fixed paradigm item. Pair reflexive pronouns (ἐμαυτοῦ/σεαυτοῦ/ἑαυτοῦ) and the reciprocal ἀλλήλων in short clauses showing person agreement with the subject; avoid introducing new tense-moods (e.g., no perfect/pluperfect) or unrelated pronoun classes in this lesson's exercises.

chapters.title: More Nouns of the Third Declension; Adjectives of the Third Declension in -ης, -ες

concepts.name: Third declension nouns: χάρις-type (dental stem, -ν accusative), πόλις-type (ι/εω-stem), γένος-type (neuter σ-stem), βασιλεύς-type (ευ-stem)
Third declension adjectives in -ης, -ες (ἀληθής, πλήρης)

chapters.notes: Drill the four third-declension noun patterns introduced (χάρις, πόλις, γένος, βασιλεύς) and the -ης/-ες adjective ἀληθής across nominative/genitive/dative/accusative singular and plural, since genitive singular plus gender is the key to recognizing each; verb forms should stay within previously covered tenses/moods (this lesson introduces no new verb morphology), and πατήρ/ἀνήρ/μήτηρ declension should be treated as review rather than new material.

chapters.title: Declension of πᾶς, πολύς, μέγας, and Numerals; Attributive and Substantive Uses of Prepositional Phrases and of the Genitive; Accusative of Extent of Time and Space

concepts.name: Irregular declension of πᾶς, πολύς, μέγας
Cardinal numerals and their declension (εἷς, δύο, τρεῖς, τέσσαρες, etc.)
Attributive/substantive prepositional phrases and genitive; accusative of extent of time and space

chapters.notes: Drill πᾶς/πολύς/μέγας in both predicate (πᾶσα ἡ πόλις) and attributive (ἡ πᾶσα πόλις) positions, plus numeral agreement with nouns; favor attributive prepositional-phrase and genitive substantive constructions (οἱ ἐν τῇ πόλει, οἱ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ) and accusative-of-extent phrases (ἔμεινα ἡμέραν μίαν); avoid introducing new moods or verb tenses beyond what's already covered.
verifier_notes: Missing grammar topic: the use of πᾶς (§§367-369) — predicate vs. attributive position (πᾶσα ἡ πόλις vs. ἡ πᾶσα πόλις), πᾶς + singular = 'every', πᾶς with article + participle; the map's GK.ADJ entry covers only the declension

chapters.title: Interrogative, Indefinite, and Relative Pronouns; Deliberative Questions; Conditional Relative Clauses

concepts.name: Interrogative pronoun τίς, τί (who? which? what?)
Indefinite pronoun τις, τι (enclitic: someone, something)
Relative pronoun ὅς, ἥ, ὅ (who, which)
Indirect questions (retain mood/tense of direct question)
Deliberative questions (subjunctive expecting an imperative-type answer)
Conditional relative clauses (-ever clauses with ἄν/ἐάν + subjunctive)
Case attraction of the relative pronoun to its antecedent

chapters.notes: Practice interrogative τίς/τί, enclitic indefinite τις/τι, and relative ὅς ἥ ὅ declensions in short questions and relative clauses; contrast indirect questions (mood/tense preserved from the direct form) with deliberative subjunctive questions (τί ποιήσωμεν;). Favor -ever conditional relative clauses with ἄν/ἐάν + subjunctive (ὃς ἄν, ὅπου ἐάν, etc.) modeled on the exercise sentences, and only lightly touch relative case-attraction (§398) as an advanced aside rather than a drilled pattern.

chapters.notes: Drill present and aorist (1st and 2nd) active/middle/passive imperative paradigms of λύω and λείπω, including irregular accents on λιποῦ, εἰπέ, ἐλθέ, and the imperative of εἰμί; pair prohibition practice (μή + present imperative vs. μή + aorist subjunctive) but avoid μή + aorist imperative, which is ungrammatical. Article used as a pronoun before μέν and δέ

chapters.notes: Focus practice on δίδωμι's present, imperfect, and aorist active (indicative ἔδωκα-type but subjunctive/imperative/infinitive/participle built on the bare stem δο-), plus ἔγνων as a second-aorist paradigm; avoid the rare present/aorist middle-passive forms of δίδωμι. Drill ὁ μέν... ὁ δέ constructions where the article functions as a pronoun (not as a substantized-phrase article like οἱ ἐν τῷ οἴκῳ), and use aorist participles only for action coincident with (not prior to) the main verb.
